# 27 The Twelve-Factor App

Part of [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/Backend from First Principles|Backend from First Principles]] · Previous: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/26 Testing for Backend Engineers/26 Testing for Backend Engineers|26 Testing for Backend Engineers]] · Next: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/28 OpenAPI/28 OpenAPI|28 OpenAPI]]

Throughout this series, many rules were stated without being defended. Why does configuration go in environment variables? Why does a server bind to a port? Why do logs go to standard output? Why must processes be stateless, and why should nothing be lost when a process is killed? Most of these rules come from one source: **the Twelve-Factor App**. This lesson walks through all twelve factors: what each says, the problem it solved, where it appeared earlier in the series, and how it has aged, including the community revision in progress since 2024.

---

## 1. What the Twelve-Factor App is

The **Twelve-Factor App** is a set of **12 rules** written in **2011** by people at **Heroku**, one of the first cloud platforms.

> A twelve-factor app is a **contract between your application and the platform that runs it**. It states what must be true about your app so that **any machine, any platform and any new teammate** can **run, scale and update** it **without surprises**.

Practically every platform you deploy to today assumes you follow these rules, directly or indirectly:

- **Heroku**, which wrote them,
- **Docker** and **Kubernetes**,
- Render, Railway, Fly.io, Google Cloud Run, AWS App Runner, Vercel, Netlify…

When a platform says *"we inject configuration through the environment"* or *"write your logs to stdout and we'll collect them"*, that comes from these rules. Many of them are now so standard that people follow them **without knowing the source**, which is a good sign. Follow the factors and every platform becomes easy to work with, because you're not fighting its expectations.

This lesson is partly **history** and partly a **map** of a contract you're probably already following.

---

## 2. Scope

- **In scope:** apps that **run as a service**, such as web apps, APIs, anything deployed somewhere and reachable over a network, in **any language**, with **any database or queue**.
- **Out of scope:** desktop software and mobile apps.
- The factors are about the **interface between the app and the platform**. They aren't a list of every good software practice: principles like **DRY** ("don't repeat yourself") or **KISS** ("keep it simple, stupid") aren't factors.
- This lesson doesn't go deep into Kubernetes operations or microservice architecture.

---

## 3. Where it came from: the snowflake-server era

### Who wrote it

In 2011, **Heroku** was about three years old. It was a **Platform as a Service (PaaS)**: you give the platform your **code**, and it handles everything else (building it, preparing the environment and configuration, connecting databases, networking) until your app is **live** on the internet at a domain name.

Running a PaaS gave Heroku a unique view: they had watched **huge numbers of apps** being deployed, scaled, breaking and getting corrupted, across many languages and frameworks. **Adam Wiggins**, a Heroku co-founder, wrote the recurring patterns down as twelve factors and published them at **12factor.net** in 2011.

### What deployment looked like then

To put an app on the internet, someone would:

1. **rent a server** from a hosting provider, or use a **physical machine in the office** (AWS existed, but cloud wasn't yet the default),
2. **install the operating system by hand** (e.g. Ubuntu),
3. **install the language runtime** by hand (Java, Python, …),
4. **install the database** and supporting libraries,
5. **copy the app onto the machine**, often over **FTP** (File Transfer Protocol),
6. **edit config files directly on the server** over **SSH**.

Each server built this way was a **snowflake**: **unique, hand-built and impossible to reproduce**.

- Repeating the steps, even from a written manual, would likely differ somewhere.
- If the machine died, you started from scratch, from memory or the manual.
- A **new developer** could take **days** to get the app running on their laptop, and even then it didn't match production. Hence the famous phrase **"it works on my machine"**.
- Teams **froze all other work** for deployment days.

### Software erosion

The document calls this **software erosion**: an app slowly **stops working even though nobody changed its code**. For example:

- the operating system gets **patched**,
- **another app on the same server** upgrades a shared library and breaks yours,
- the person who set up the infrastructure **leaves** without documenting every manual change, which is nearly impossible to track anyway.

**The twelve factors are defences against erosion.**

---

## 4. The 2024 open-source revision

The document was effectively **frozen for 13 years**. Its footer says "last updated 2017", and that update was small. Meanwhile **containers, Kubernetes, serverless and managed cloud services** took over.

In **November 2024**, Heroku (now owned by **Salesforce**) **open-sourced** the document:

- it moved it into a **public repository under a neutral organisation**,
- it wrote a **governance document**,
- it invited maintainers from other companies, including **AWS** and **Google Cloud**, to revise it as a community.

The announcement was made on stage at **KubeCon** (November 2024).

The revision is happening in public on a branch called **`next`**:

- It **keeps all twelve names** and their **one-line mottos**.
- It rewrites each factor into a **numbered list of principles**, separating **timeless** ideas from **2011-era** details and adding **modern** guidance.
- At the time of recording, the live site still showed the **2011 text**, and the rewrite was an **unmerged working draft**.

So for each factor below: **the original 2011 idea first**, then **what the rewrite changes** or how the factor has aged.

---

## 5. Factor 1: Codebase

> **One codebase tracked in revision control, many deploys.**

### Part 1: tracked in revision control

Obvious today. Development without **Git** and GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket is hard to imagine. In 2011 it needed saying: many production apps were **a folder on someone's computer** or a zip file named `final_v2_really_final.zip`, emailed between teammates.

### Part 2: many deploys

A **deploy** is **one running instance of the app**: production is a deploy, staging is a deploy, and some teams create a **deploy per pull request**.

**Same codebase, different deploys.** What differs between them? **Never the code.** It's the **config** (factor 3): production talks to a real database, while your laptop talks to a Postgres container.

Different deploys **may run different commits**, but always **from the same repository**:

```text
Repository at commit 100
├── production   → commit 97   (deployed last Friday)
├── staging      → commit 99   (being tested for tomorrow's release)
└── your laptop  → commit 100 + 2 unpushed commits
```

*(Illustrative.)*

On release day, staging moves to 100, then production moves to 100. Nothing about the deploys changed except **which commit** each runs.

**Test:** if you can't describe each environment as *"this codebase at commit X"*, something is going wrong.

### Two boundaries

- **Several codebases** don't make **an app**; they make a **distributed system** of apps, and **each app** should follow the twelve factors.
- **Two apps sharing code by copy-paste** is a violation. Shared code should become a **library** used through the **dependency manager** (factor 2).

### In 2026: monorepos

Some people read this factor as "monorepos are an anti-pattern". The creator disagrees. The test is **one codebase ↔ one app**. A monorepo that builds five apps is effectively **five codebases that happen to live in one repository**, each following the factors. What the factor forbids is **the same app living in two places** (copy-paste code), not many apps in one repository.

---

## 6. Factor 2: Dependencies

> **Explicitly declare and isolate dependencies.**

### Declare

Somewhere in the repository, a file (a **manifest**) lists **completely and accurately** every library the app needs:

| Language | Manifest | Lock file |
|---|---|---|
| Node.js | `package.json` | `package-lock.json` |
| Go | `go.mod` | `go.sum` |
| Python | `requirements.txt` / `pyproject.toml` | e.g. `poetry.lock`, `uv.lock` |
| Ruby | `Gemfile` | `Gemfile.lock` |

**Without a manifest**, a new teammate or a new laptop has to read every import statement, guess versions and untangle conflicts: days of setup. **With one**, setup is **one command** (`npm install`, `bundle install`…). The 2011 text used Ruby's `Gemfile` with `bundle install`, since Rails was very popular then.

Today the idea is stronger thanks to **lock files**. A manifest often specifies **version ranges**; a lock file records the **exact version** of every library **and of every library those libraries depend on**. So the app installs the same versions months or years later.

### Isolate

Declaring isn't enough if the app can **see things outside the declaration**.

**Example:** your `requirements.txt` asks for `requests` version 2, but the app runs against the **system Python**, where another tool installed `requests` version 1. The import finds the **system copy first**, so the declaration was ignored.

- **Declare without isolating** → it won't work the same everywhere.
- **Isolate without declaring** → you'll spend days reproducing versions.

The 2011 text named **`bundle exec`** (Ruby) and **`virtualenv`** (Python) as isolation tools: the app sees **only its declared dependencies**.

### System tools leak too

Apps also shouldn't rely on **system tools** being present. Example: an image-resizing backend **shells out** to **ImageMagick**:

- on a Mac, Homebrew installed **ImageMagick 7**, whose main command is `magick`,
- on the Ubuntu server, apt installed **ImageMagick 6**, whose command is `convert`, with different defaults.

The same code does different things on the two machines, because across a **major version** these are effectively different programs with breaking changes. The 2011 advice was to **vendor** such tools into the app (ship them with it).

### In 2026: containers

**Containers** changed this factor completely. A **Docker image** freezes not only libraries but also the **operating system, system tools and runtime**, which is the ultimate declaration and isolation. That's why people say **Docker practically solved factor 2**.

---

## 7. Factor 3: Config

> **Store config in the environment.**

One of the most quoted and most argued factors. (See also [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/17 Configuration Management/17 Configuration Management|lesson 17]].)

### What counts as config?

**Config is everything likely to vary between deploys.**

| Thing | On your laptop | In production |
|---|---|---|
| Database URL | `localhost`, Postgres in Docker | Amazon RDS over a private network |
| Email | Provider's **sandbox** API | Real sending |
| Object storage | Local **MinIO** | AWS **S3** |
| Redis | Local container | Managed Redis |

The **code** is the same; only these values change.

### Why keep config out of code: the open-source test

> **Could you open-source your codebase right now without leaking a single credential?**

Not *would* you, but *could* you. If the answer is no, config is living in your code.

### Why environment variables?

1. **Easy to change between deploys** without editing files.
2. **Can't be committed to the repository by accident**, which is how credentials leak every day.
3. **Language- and OS-agnostic.** Environment variables are an operating-system feature, so they work the same for Go, Node.js, Rust, Python or a bash script.

The alternatives of the time were framework-specific formats (Java **properties files**, Rails's **`config/database.yml`**), which regularly ended up committed to source control, credentials and all.

### Example from the series' own codebase

In the **Tasker** task-management app built in an earlier video, the `config` package declares all configuration as **one Go struct**, with blocks for server, database, auth, Redis, email, AWS, observability and cron: **about 38 values**, all loaded from **environment variables** with a `TASKER_` prefix (e.g. `TASKER_SERVER_PORT`, `TASKER_DATABASE_HOST`). The Git history shows the **values** changed often (new integrations, timeouts, hosts) while the **code that reads them** barely changed.

**Things that change at different rates shouldn't live in the same place.**

### Don't group config into named environments

The 2011 text warns against files like `config/environments/staging.rb` and `production.rb`. That **doesn't scale**: a deploy that is "like staging but with a different database" (e.g. for a PR) needs **more code**.

Instead, each config value should be an **independent, granular environment variable**, never tied to a "mode" name. You **compose a new deploy by setting values**, not by choosing a mode. The rewrite keeps this: environment variables are **granular controls**, never grouped as "environments".

---

## 8. Secrets: are environment variables enough?

Environment variables are great for a **database hostname**. But for a **database password**?

In **2017**, **Diogo Mónica**, who led security at **Docker**, wrote a well-known article arguing **not to put secrets in environment variables**, because **the environment leaks eventually**:

- **Child processes inherit the whole environment**, so any shell command your app starts gets every secret.
- **Crash reporters and debug pages** often **dump the whole environment**.
- On Linux, a process's environment can be read from **`/proc/<pid>/environ`** by anyone with the right access, and various tools log it.

**The better pattern for secrets:**

1. Store them in a **secret manager**, such as **HashiCorp Vault** or **AWS Parameter Store / Secrets Manager**.
2. The app **fetches them at startup** and keeps them **only in its own memory**.
3. **Rotate** and **audit** them regularly.

### Where this leaves factor 3

- **Separating config from code is non-negotiable**, then and now.
- **Environment variables** are the **right default for non-secret config**.
- For **secrets**: solo developers and small teams can reasonably use their platform's secret feature, which injects environment variables (far better than committed credentials). As the team and product grow, a **secret manager** is the **no-brainer** choice.

(Credential handling is also discussed in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/20 Backend Security/20 Backend Security#18. Misconfiguration|lesson 20]].)

---

## 9. Factor 4: Backing services

> **Treat backing services as attached resources.**

A **backing service** is **anything the app consumes over the network**:

- databases (Postgres),
- caches (Redis),
- queues,
- SMTP or email services,
- object storage (S3),
- third-party APIs (payment providers…).

**Rule:** the code must make **no distinction** between a service **you run** and one **someone else runs**. Each is an **attached resource**, reached through a **resource handle** (**URL + credentials**), which lives in **config** (factor 3).

**Test from the 2011 text:** you should be able to swap your local Postgres for a managed one (**Neon**, **PlanetScale**, **Supabase**, **Amazon RDS**…) **without changing a single line of code**, only the handle.

### A resource handle

```text
postgres://app_user:s3cr3t@db.internal.example.com:5432/tasker
└──┬───┘   └───┬──┘ └─┬──┘ └───────────┬──────────┘ └┬─┘ └─┬──┘
 scheme      user  password           host          port  database
```

*(Illustrative.)*

- **Scheme**: `postgres` means "speaks the Postgres wire protocol".
- **Credentials**: user and password.
- **Host** and **port** (Postgres's default is **5432**).
- **Database name**.

One string holds everything the app needs to attach the resource.

### How it aged: very well

In 2011 this was **eccentric**. Most people ran the **server and database on the same machine**, so "the database is someone else's computer, reached by URL" was hard to relate to. Fifteen years later it's universal: managed Postgres (RDS, Neon, PlanetScale), managed Redis, S3 for files, **Resend** and similar services for email. Running the app and database on the same machine is now considered an **anti-pattern for scaling**. This factor was close to a **prediction**.

---

## 10. Factor 5: Build, release, run

> **Strictly separate build and run stages.**

A CI/CD pipeline roughly has three stages:

| Stage | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Build** | Code at a **specific commit** (from source control, not FTP) | Fetch dependencies (factor 2), compile if needed → one executable bundle, the **build**: a single Go binary, a Node.js app plus `node_modules`, or a **container image**. **Contains code + dependencies, never config.** |
| **Release** | A build + **one deploy's config** (production, staging, a PR preview…) | A **release**: an exact build plus exact config, ready to run. Same build + production config = production release; + staging config = staging release. |
| **Run** | A release | **Launch processes** from it |

### Why be so strict? Two benefits

**1. Instant, reliable rollbacks.** Builds are **immutable**, and releases form an **append-only ledger**: each has an **ID** (timestamp or incrementing number) and is **never modified**.

```text
Release 100  = build @ commit 97 + config v1        (afternoon)
Release 101  = build @ commit 97 + config v2        (DB password rotated)
Release 102  = build @ commit 98 + config v2        (new code) → errors spike!
→ roll back: re-run Release 101                     (seconds)
```

*(Illustrative timeline.)*

When release 102 causes errors and users are complaining, you don't debug in production. You **re-run release 101**, which takes seconds, then debug 102 calmly. That works only because **release 101 still means exactly what it meant two hours ago**: same build, same config. Heroku releases, Docker image tags and Kubernetes rollouts all follow this pattern.

**2. No editing code on production servers.** Code enters the pipeline **only at the build stage**, so there's **no path from a running machine back into a build**. In the snowflake era, people would SSH in, **hot-patch** the code and reload, and production quietly drifted away from the repository. Strict stages make that impossible.

### The rewrite

It makes explicit what 2011 implied: **each release must be a unique, immutable snapshot**.

---

## 11. Factor 6: Processes

> **Execute the app as one or more stateless processes.**

Processes must **remember nothing between requests**. This is the **statelessness** property that has come up throughout the series (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2#1. Statelessness: the key to horizontal scaling|lesson 21.2]]).

- **Share nothing**: processes share no memory and no disk.
- Anything that must persist goes into a **stateful backing service** (factor 4).
- Assume **any request can be served by any process**, and **any process can disappear at any moment**.

### What a process may hold

**Memory and local disk as a short-lived cache for a single transaction.** Example: download a file to a temporary folder, process it, write the result to the database. That's fine, because **nothing afterwards expects the file to exist**. It becomes a problem only when a **future request or process depends on it** (compare [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/23 Object Storage Part 1/23 Object Storage Part 1#3. Problem 1: the server's disk is ephemeral|lesson 23]]).

### Sticky sessions are a violation

The scenario:

1. The app stores **logged-in sessions in process memory** (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/08 Authentication and Authorization/08 Authentication and Authorization#3. Three building blocks: sessions, JWTs, cookies|lesson 08]]).
2. It's scaled to three instances behind a load balancer.
3. A user logs in on instance 1, and the next request lands on instance 2, which has never heard of them. They're randomly **logged out**.

The workaround is **sticky sessions**: the load balancer remembers which instance each user belongs to and always routes them there. The factor calls this a **violation**:

- **Kill an instance**, and all its users are logged out.
- **Add an instance** to handle load, and it gets **no existing users**.

Stickiness defeats the point of having several instances.

**Fix:** sessions are **state**, and state goes into a **backing service**: Redis, Postgres, whatever fits your latency needs.

### The exception: real-time connections

A **WebSocket** lives in **one process's memory** and only that instance can talk to the user. That breaks statelessness, and [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/25 Real-Time Backends/25 Real-Time Backends#14. Many instances: a connection is state|lesson 25]] worked around it with **pub/sub**.

The creator's view: statelessness is the **default everywhere**, but you may break it **when the feature itself is the state**, as with real-time connections.

**Rule of thumb:** if you **can't kill any process at any moment without a user losing data**, you have state where it doesn't belong.

---

## 12. Halfway recap

Six factors in, the app has gained real freedom:

- **its code** lives in one repository (1),
- **its dependencies** are declared and isolated (2),
- **every difference between deploys** lives in the environment (3),
- **its neighbours** (backing services) are attached through handles (4),
- **it reaches production** through build → release → run (5),
- **it runs** as **disposable, forgetful processes** (6).

---

## 13. Factor 7: Port binding

> **Export services via port binding.**

This sounds obvious today, but in 2011:

- A **PHP** app didn't run by itself. **Apache** ran, and the PHP app was a **module loaded inside Apache**.
- A **Java** app didn't run by itself. **Tomcat** ran, and the app was a file dropped into Tomcat's folder.

The **web server was the program**, and your app was a **guest** inside it. The web server's version and configuration became part of your app's runtime environment, living on the physical server. That's **erosion** again.

**The factor:** the app must be **completely self-contained**. It **brings its own HTTP server as a library** (declared through factor 2's manifest) and **exports itself** by **binding to a port** and listening for connections.

- In development: `http://localhost:8080`.
- In production: a **routing layer**, such as a reverse proxy or load balancer, forwards the public hostname to the process's port.

**Consequence:** any app that binds a port can be a **backing service for another app**. Databases, caches and email services all bind ports. Locally they're on `localhost`; in production you just swap the handles to someone else's machine in the cloud. Same pattern throughout.

### How it aged: serverless

An **AWS Lambda** function **doesn't bind a port**; the platform **calls a function you export** (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2#12. Serverless|lesson 21.2]]). The 2011 assumption that services are long-running and port-bound didn't hold for everything.

The rewrite keeps **port binding** as the headline but generalises it: the app is **self-contained** and **exports its service through a declared interface**. That covers both a port-bound server and a serverless function.

---

## 14. Factor 8: Concurrency

> **Scale out via the process model.**

### Before

Each runtime scaled its own way:

- **Java:** one **huge JVM process** grabbed a big block of RAM at startup and **multiplexed with threads** inside itself.
- **PHP:** the opposite. **Apache spawned small child processes** on demand.

### The factor

Make the **process a first-class citizen**: design the app to **scale by running more processes**, inspired by the **Unix model** of service **daemons**. Different kinds of work get different **process types**:

| Process type | Handles |
|---|---|
| **web** | HTTP requests |
| **worker** | Heavy background jobs: video encoding, image resizing… (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/14 Task Queues and Background Jobs/14 Task Queues and Background Jobs|lesson 14]]) |
| **scheduler / clock** | Timed work, e.g. emails sent at midnight |

Each type **scales independently** by running more or fewer copies.

### Example: a food-delivery app

Assume every process uses about **500 MB**:

| Time | Combined web + worker process | Separate process types |
|---|---|---|
| **Lunch rush** (many orders, few jobs) | Need 10 web → must run 10 combined copies → workers also ×10 → about **10 GB**, half of it idle | **10 web + 2 workers** → about **6 GB** |
| **Night** (few orders, many batch jobs) | — | **5 web + 20 workers** |

*(Illustrative numbers.)*

The **type and count** of processes, e.g. `web=3, worker=2`, is called the **process formation**. The term is still used: a **Procfile** declares process types, and a **Kubernetes** deployment's `replicas: 3` is a formation written in YAML.

```text
# Procfile (illustrative)
web:       ./bin/server
worker:    ./bin/worker
scheduler: ./bin/scheduler
```

### Notes

- **Threads are allowed inside a process**: JVM threads, Go goroutines, Node's event loop (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/22 Concurrency and Parallelism/22 Concurrency and Parallelism|lesson 22]]). But the **unit of scaling is the process**. One machine can only grow so far vertically; share-nothing processes can spread across **many machines**.
- **A twelve-factor app never daemonises itself or writes a PID file.** Managing the process's lifetime is the job of the **platform**: the OS, systemd, Kubernetes or a process manager. The app just **runs in the foreground**.

### How it aged

**Orchestrators** (Kubernetes and others) now run most of the internet: you **declare a formation** and the platform starts, kills and restarts containers to maintain it. The factor isn't outdated; it was **adopted so thoroughly** that you rarely think about it, unless you deploy straight onto an OS with systemd, where it still applies directly.

---

## 15. Factor 9: Disposability

> **Maximize robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown.**

Processes should be **disposable**: they can be **started or stopped at a moment's notice**, with nothing bad happening either way. (Covered in depth in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/19 Graceful Shutdown/19 Graceful Shutdown|lesson 19]].)

### Why it matters

Platforms start and stop processes **constantly**:

- **scaling** adds processes at any moment,
- **deployments** kill old processes and start new ones from the new image,
- orchestrators **move processes between machines** whenever they like.

Deploying **5 times a week to 10 instances** means **50 stops and 50 starts** a week from deployments alone. A process dying is **normal**, part of the release lifecycle, **not an incident**.

### Fast startup

If boot takes **60 seconds**:

- a rolling deploy of 10 instances, one at a time, takes **10 minutes**,
- the autoscaler reacts to a traffic spike **a minute late**.

With **2-second** startup, both are negligible. Aim for **a few seconds**.

### Graceful shutdown

**Web processes**, on **SIGTERM**, follow the lifecycle from [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/19 Graceful Shutdown/19 Graceful Shutdown#6. Step 1: connection draining|lesson 19]]:

1. **stop accepting** new requests,
2. **finish** in-flight requests,
3. **exit**.

Otherwise every deployment gives in-flight users **errors**.

**Worker processes**, on shutdown, **return the current job to the queue** instead of discarding it. That requires jobs to be **re-entrant**: an interrupted job must leave **no dirty state**, so running it again is safe. You get this by:

- wrapping the work in a **transaction**, or
- making it **idempotent**: running it twice gives the same result as once (e.g. detecting already-done work and skipping it).

### Robust against sudden death

SIGTERM is the **polite** case: you get a grace period (often about 30 seconds) to wrap up. But a process can also die **without warning**: a hardware failure, or the container is **OOM-killed** (out of memory). So design for a process being **killed mid-instruction at any time**.

The document points to **crash-only design**: if your system **survives crashes** correctly, you barely need a separate graceful-shutdown path, because **the crash path is the shutdown path**.

---

## 16. Factor 10: Dev/prod parity

> **Keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible.**

The document names **three gaps** between development and production:

| Gap | Traditional app | Twelve-factor app |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | Code written today reaches production next week, bundled with lots of other changes | Deploy **hours** after writing |
| **Personnel** | Developers write code; ops engineers deploy and see the errors | **The people who write the code deploy it** and watch its logs |
| **Tools** | Laptop (macOS/Windows, different stack) vs Linux servers with external backing services | Keep the environments **as similar as possible** |

Closing the gaps makes **continuous deployment** smooth. The **time and personnel gaps** are largely closed today; the **tools gap** still exists.

### The classic tools-gap trap: SQLite in dev, Postgres in prod

**ORMs** (Drizzle and Prisma in Node.js, GORM in Go, SQLAlchemy in Python) abstract the database, so it's tempting to use lightweight **SQLite** locally and **PostgreSQL** in production. But behaviour differs:

| | PostgreSQL | SQLite |
|---|---|---|
| `LIKE` | **Case-sensitive** (`ILIKE` is the case-insensitive version) | **Case-insensitive by default** for ASCII letters |

A search feature built and tested on SQLite will **behave differently in production**, with **no error, warning or log**. Behaviour just silently changes.

**The factor's advice:** use the **same backing services** (database, cache, queue) in development, staging and production. Today there's little excuse: **one command starts a container** locally. (Compare testing against a real database in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/26 Testing for Backend Engineers/26 Testing for Backend Engineers#17. Databases: test against the real thing|lesson 26]].)

### In 2026: not so clean

For a while, Docker and Docker Compose made local and production nearly identical. Then teams moved to **managed services**. **AWS DynamoDB**, for example, is proprietary: you can't run the real thing locally. Emulators such as **LocalStack** imitate many AWS services, but they're **not the same implementation**, and they only reproduce **documented** behaviour.

There's no simple rule like "avoid managed services". They offer real benefits: easier scaling and **lower operational cost**. **Weigh the trade-off**: if a managed service's benefits are large enough, accept some dev/prod difference.

## 17. Factor 11: Logs

> **Treat logs as event streams.**

We tend to think of logs as **files**, but the **file was never the log**; it's just one place logs can end up. A log is a **stream of time-ordered events** that flows **as long as the app runs**, with no fixed beginning or end.

**The factor:** a twelve-factor app **doesn't concern itself with routing or storing** its log stream: no log-file paths, no log rotation. It writes every event, **unbuffered, to stdout**. The **execution environment** (platform or orchestrator) **captures** the stream and decides where it goes: a file, or a **log drain** (an external service for storage and analysis).

### Why

1. **No code changes per environment.** Logging destinations become the platform's concern and config. In 2011, stdout often went to **syslog**; today it goes to tools like **Loki** or **Datadog**, but the pattern is the same.
2. **Streams compose; files don't.**
   - **Laptop:** you read the logs live in your terminal.
   - **Container:** the runtime captures the stream, **tags each line with the process it came from**, and hands it to a **collector**.
   - **Production:** the platform **merges the streams of all instances into one time-ordered stream**, so you don't care which instance logged what, only **when** it happened.

### How it aged

Today **observability** means **logs, metrics and traces** (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability#2. Short definitions|lesson 18]]). The 2011 text mentions only logs, because metrics and tracing weren't common practice then. Treat them as **additions**; the factor doesn't forbid them.

## 18. Factor 12: Admin processes

> **Run admin/management tasks as one-off processes.**

A **one-off process** runs **once**, **alongside** the app's long-running processes, and then **exits**. Examples:

- a **database migration** (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/12 Databases with Postgres/12 Databases with Postgres#9. Migrations|lesson 12]]),
- a script that **fixes some data** in production.

**The rule:** one-off admin processes must run in an **identical environment** to the regular processes:

- the **same codebase**, at the **same commit** (shipped in the same release),
- the **same config**,
- the **same dependency isolation**.

**Why so strict?** In the old way, someone would **SSH into the production server and run an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` by hand**, with no code review, no record and no log. Production drifted away from what the code and documentation said. Migrations are the classic well-behaved example: they ship **with the code** and run **as a one-off process before the app starts**.

## 19. Demo: several factors in practice

**Demo (shown in the lesson):** the series' **task app** backend, running on a Linux machine reached over SSH.

- **Process types:** it's driven by a **Procfile** (Heroku's invention for declaring process types) with a **`web`** process type.
- **Process formation:** a process manager, **Overmind**, starts the formation.
- **Boot order:** a **schema check**, then the **background job server**, then the server **binds to its assigned port**.
- **Logs:** the log stream goes to **stdout**.
- **One-off process:** in a second pane, an **auto-archive** admin task runs from the **same code, config and environment**, then **exits**.
- **Graceful shutdown:** on **Ctrl-C**, the **connection pool closes**, the **job server waits for its workers to finish**, and the process reports a **clean exit**.

This shows **port binding (7)**, the **process model (8)**, **disposability (9)**, **logs to stdout (11)** and **admin processes (12)**.

## 20. All twelve at a glance

| # | Factor | One line | Where it stands today |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Codebase** | One repo per app, many deploys | Universal; monorepos are fine (one codebase per app) |
| 2 | **Dependencies** | Declare (manifest + lock file) and isolate | Containers "practically solved" it |
| 3 | **Config** | In the environment, granular, never in code | Still core; use a **secret manager** for secrets |
| 4 | **Backing services** | Attached resources via URL + credentials | Aged very well: managed services everywhere |
| 5 | **Build, release, run** | Strict stages; immutable releases | Rewrite makes immutability explicit |
| 6 | **Processes** | Stateless, share nothing | Default; real-time connections are the conscious exception |
| 7 | **Port binding** | Self-contained, exports via a port | Generalised to "a declared interface" for serverless |
| 8 | **Concurrency** | Scale by process type and count (formation) | Absorbed into orchestrators (`replicas:`) |
| 9 | **Disposability** | Fast startup, graceful shutdown, survive sudden death | Essential with frequent deploys and autoscaling |
| 10 | **Dev/prod parity** | Close the time, personnel and tools gaps | Tools gap persists with proprietary managed services |
| 11 | **Logs** | Unbuffered event stream to stdout | Extended by metrics and traces (observability) |
| 12 | **Admin processes** | One-off tasks in an identical environment | Migrations as one-off processes are standard |

*(This table summarises the points made factor by factor above.)*

## Key takeaways

- The Twelve-Factor App (Heroku, 2011) is a **contract between an app and its platform**, and a defence against **software erosion** and **snowflake servers**.
- It was open-sourced in **2024** for a community rewrite that separates timeless principles from 2011 details.
- **Code** is shared by all deploys; **config** makes each deploy different, so keep them strictly apart.
- **Dependencies** must be declared **and** isolated; containers take this to the extreme.
- **Backing services** are attached via handles in config: swap them without code changes.
- **Build → release → run** with **immutable releases** gives instant rollbacks and no hot-patching.
- **Stateless, share-nothing, disposable processes**, scaled by **type and count**, started quickly and stopped gracefully, robust against sudden death.
- **Keep dev and prod alike**, especially backing services (the SQLite-vs-Postgres `LIKE` trap).
- **Logs are streams to stdout**; the platform routes them.
- **Admin tasks** run as **one-off processes** from the same release and config.
